main.text: [II, 838] CHAPTER 16. [col. 238]
The very obscure passage on the ostrich, Job 39:16 var. 13., is explained

In Iobi XXXIX, 16. (var. 13.) the ostrich is described in six verses, of which the interpreters explain the last five after a fashion. But in the first they are so stuck that there is scarcely any passage of Scripture that is less understood. Nowhere is there greater disagreement among them, as will be clear from a comparison, which I am pleased to set out here so that the matter may be clearer to the reader. That verse, then, of which I speak, the Septuagint renders thus: Πτέρυξ τερπομένων νεέλασσα, ἐὰν συλλάβῃ ἀσίδα, καὶ νέσσα· [Pteryx terpomenōn neelassa, ean syllabē asida, kai nessa] The wing of those that rejoice is neelassa, if it has conceived asida and nessa. And Aquila: Πτερύγιον αἰνέντων συναναπλέκει . . . . ἐρώδιος, καὶ ἱέραξ· [Pterygion ainentōn synanaplekei . . . . erōdios, kai hierax] The heron and the hawk together entwine . . . . the wing of those that praise. And Symmachus: Πτερὸν ἀγλαισμοῦ περιφύεται, εἰ ἐναγκαλίσεται ὁ κύκνος πτίλους αὐτοῦ· [Pteron aglaismou periphyetai, ei enankalisetai ho kyknos ptilous autou] A wing of splendour grows round about, if the swan should clasp its feathers in its arms. And Jerome: The feather of the ostrich is like the feathers of the heron and the hawk. And the Syriac, which the Arabic mostly follows: ܒܓܦ ܡܫܒܚܢܐ ܡܬܪܘܡܐ ܘܦܪܚܐ ܘܐܬܝܐ ܘܡܩܢܢܐ [בגף משבחנא מתרומא ופרחא ואתיא ומקננא], With wings of praises it is lifted up, and flies, and comes, and nests. And the Chaldee: גדפא דתרנגול דמשבחא ומקלסא ואין אברא דחוריתא ונוציציתא, The wing of the cock, which praises and celebrates: and is it the wing of the stork and the hawk? These versions of the ancients not only differ from one another δὶς διὰ πασῶν [dis dia pasōn], but most of them are also absurd and incongruous, and attribute to the sacred writer things that yield no suitable sense. Nor is there more agreement among some of the moderns. For Castalio [=Sebastian Castellio, Latin Bible (1551)] has: Are the wings of the ostrich nobler, or the feathers and plumage of the stork? And Arias [=Benito Arias Montano, the interlinear Latin of the Antwerp Polyglot], quite differently and with no sense: The wing of those that exult is glad; or the feather of the stork, and plumage? And Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible], differently again: Would you give the wing to the peacocks to exult in, or the feather of the stork, or to the ostrich? Differently also the vernacular versions, I mean the French, English, Dutch and Italian: Have you given to the peacocks, or Do the peacocks have splendid wings through your work, or wings in which they exult? Have you given feathers and plumage to the ostrich? Since there is no leisure to examine each of these, it will suffice to deal with our vulgar version, which itself also does not seem accurate enough. For there are chiefly two things we find wanting in it. One, that it supplies too much that is not usually supplied, namely at the very beginning of the verse אם נתת, Have you given?, and the letter Lamed, the mark of the dative, before the words רננים and חסידה. The other, that it explains רננים renanim as peacocks, and חסידה chasida as ostrich; with neither of which can I agree. I shall therefore say what I think about the meaning of each word, so that the true meaning of the whole verse may emerge from it.

[II, 839] The former, namely רננים renanim, could, while the vowels were absent, be read ronenim, that is, singing, praising, exulting, etc. Hence arose those versions, wing of the praising, wing of the rejoicing, etc., in the Elders [=the translators of the Septuagint], Aquila and others. But the Chaldee and Jerome, even though the points were lacking, nevertheless rightly gathered from the sequence of the words that רננים is something else, namely the name of a bird. And all the Hebrews embrace the same opinion, although they cannot determine which birds are called רננים renanim. The Chaldee renders it cock, not the common one, but תרנגול דמשבחא ומקלסא, the cock which praises and celebrates God. Of which the same translator speaks on the words of Job cursing his day, Job 3:7. Let no song come into it: לא תעול רננא דתרנגול ברא למקלסה בה, Let not the song of the wild cock come to praise in it. And on Iobi XXXVIII, 36. מי שוי בכלין חוכמתא או יהב לתרנגול ברא בינתא למקלסה למריה, Who has put wisdom in the reins? or given the wild cock understanding to praise his Lord? And on Ps 50:11. גלין קדמי כל מיני עופא דפרחין באויר שמיא ותרנגול ברא דקרסולי שרין בארעא ורישיה מטי בשמיא מרנן קדמי, Known to me are all the kinds of birds that fly in the air of the heavens; and the wild cock, whose feet stand on the earth and whose head reaches to heaven, sings before me. Of this same cock Mahomet speaks thus in the Chronica Espahan: لله ديك ابيض جناحاه موشيا بالزبرجد والياقوت واللولو له جناح بالمشرق وجناح بالمغرب وراسه تحت العرش وقوايمه في الهوي يوذن في كل سحر فيسمع اهل السموات والارض الا الثقلين الجن والانس فعند ذلك تجيبه ديوك الارض فاذا دنا يوم القيمة يقال الله تعالي له ضم جناحيك وغض صوتك فيعلم اهل السموات والارض الا الثقلين ان الساعة قد اقتربت [li-llāh dīk abyaḍ janāḥāhu mawshiyyā bi-l-zabarjad wa-l-yāqūt wa-l-luʾluʾ lahu janāḥ bi-l-mashriq wa-janāḥ bi-l-maghrib wa-raʾsuhu taḥt al-ʿarsh wa-qawāʾimuhu fī al-hawā yuʾadhdhin fī kull saḥar fa-yasmaʿ ahl al-samawāt wa-l-arḍ illā al-thaqalayn al-jinn wa-l-ins fa-ʿinda dhālika tujībuhu duyūk al-arḍ fa-idhā danā yawm al-qiyāma yaqūl Allāh taʿālā lahu ḍumma janāḥayka wa-ghuḍḍ ṣawtaka fa-yaʿlam ahl al-samawāt wa-l-arḍ illā al-thaqalayn anna al-sāʿa qad iqtarabat] God has a white cock, whose wings are adorned with emeralds, carbuncles and pearls. One of them is spread towards the east, the other towards the west; its head is beneath the throne of glory, and its feet in the air. Every morning it calls to prayer, and all the inhabitants of heaven and earth hear it, except men and [col. 240] demons. Therefore the cocks of the earth answer it. And when the day of judgement is at hand, God Most High will say to it: Draw in your wings and restrain your voice, so that all the inhabitants of heaven and earth, except men and demons, may know that the hour is at hand. Because this fabulous cock is imagined to praise God at fixed hours, whence it is called מרנן merannen, praising, Ps 50:11, and its song רננא renana, Job 3:7, the circumcised doctors would have the same cock signified by the word רננים renanim in the passage with which we are dealing. But it is strange that that cock should be called by a plural word, since it is unique. The same objection could be raised against R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)]. For to him רננים renanim is that bird which in the [II, 840] Mishnah is called בר יוכני bor juchne, or son of the nest, of which we spoke above ^{a)}; and it too is singular and unique in its kind.

But, bidding farewell to these trifles, let us hear others. R. Levi doubts whether both words, כנף רננים canaph renanim, or only the latter, belong to the name of this bird. Aben Ezra [=Abraham ibn Ezra] holds that it is called renanim from the verb רנן ranan, which means to sing, בעבור נועם קולו, on account of the elegance of its voice. And in Pomarius [=David de Pomis, Ṣemaḥ David (Venice 1587)] some declare it to be a bird שמתפאר בקולו הערב רוסיניולו בלעז, which displays the sweetness of its voice, called in Italian rossignuolo, that is, nightingale. Yet he himself prefers the peacock to be understood, שמתפאר בראיית כנפיו, which glories in the display of its feathers. And between the two opinions Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim] is so undecided that he leans rather to the latter. Perhaps, he says, it is a songbird, and so called from the modulation of its song: או מרנן ומתעלס בכנפיו שהם יפות כמו הטווס ואולי הוא הוא, or it is a bird which rejoices and exults because of the beauty of its feathers, like the peacock, and perhaps it is the peacock itself. This opinion, although new and put forward only hesitantly, has nevertheless been received by our scholars with the greatest applause, as being truer than what happened at the Sagra [the proverb for a thing beyond doubt]. Thus Pagninus [=Santes Pagnino, Latin Bible (1528) and Thesaurus linguae sanctae] here has The peacock exults in its wings. So also Mercerus [=Jean Mercier (d. 1570), commentaries on Job and Proverbs]. And Junius, the wing of peacocks is to be exulted in. And all the vernacular versions in all languages that I have been able to come across follow the same. For all who have known the peacock, whether from books or from αὐτοψίᾳ [autopsia], know that it displays its feathers with pomp and pride, and so exults and prides itself in their beauty. Hence Ovid in book 1 of the Art [of Love]:
The bird of Juno displays its feathers when praised: If you watch in silence, it hides away its riches.
And in On Facial Cosmetics:
The bird of Juno spreads before man its praised feathers, and the bird is very proud of its beauty.
And in the eighth Fable of book 13 of the Metamorphoses, on Galatea:
Prouder than the praised peacock. — —

To this belong these words of Columella, book 9, chapter 11: He covers himself, as if admiring himself, with the jewelled feathers of his tail, and when he does this, he is said to "wheel." And those of Pliny, book 10, chapter 20: When praised he spreads out his jewelled colours, especially facing the sun, because thus they shine more brilliantly. And a little later: And he gathers into a heap all the eyes of his feathers, which he delights to have looked at. But it is above all the Greeks who take pleasure in this theme, and spread the sails of their eloquence as widely [II, 841] as the peacock spreads his feathers. Among them Moschus, being older, is also simpler, and has only this, Idyll. 2:
Ὄρνις ἀγαλλόμενος πτερύγων πολυανθέϊ χροιῇ, [Ornis agallomenos pterygōn polyantheï chroiē,]

A bird exulting in the flowery colour of its feathers. But Dio says far more in the Olympic oration, where he describes the peacock ἐπαφόμενον, καὶ ἐπιδεικνύοντα τὸ κάλλος τῶν πτερῶν, ὅταν ἁβρύνεται πρὸς τὴν θήλειαν, ἀνακλάσας τὴν οὐρὰν, καὶ περιστήσας αὐτῷ πανταχόθεν, ὥσπερ εὐειδὲς θέατρον, ἤ τινι γραφῇ μιμηθέντα οὐρανὸν ποικίλον ἄστροις· [epaphomenon, kai epideiknyonta to kallos tōn pterōn, hotan habrynetai pros tēn thēleian, anaklasas tēn ouran, kai peristēsas autō pantachothen, hōsper eueides theatron, ē tini graphē mimēthenta ouranon poikilon astrois] exalting himself and showing off the beauty of his feathers, when he plays the lover to the female, bending back his tail and setting it round himself on every side, like a handsome theatre, or like a painting imitating the heaven studded with stars. [col. 241] And below: Ἐν μέσῳ δὲ μάλα ἥσυχον καὶ ἀτρεμοῦντα παρέχει ἑαυτὸν θεάσασθαι, ὥσπερ ἐν πομπῇ περιστρεφόμενον· [En mesō de mala hēsychon kai atremounta parechei heauton theasasthai, hōsper en pompē peristrephomenon] In the middle he offers himself to be viewed quite still and motionless, as if carried round in a procession. In the first passage of Dio, for ἀνακλάσας τὴν οὐρὰν [anaklasas tēn ouran], the most noble Monsieur de Grentemesnil advises reading ἀνακλίσας [anaklisas] opening, or spreading out; which pleases me very much. Aelian, History of Animals, book 5, chapter 21: Ὁ ταὼς οἶδεν ὀρνίθων ὡραιότατος ὢν, καὶ ἔνθα οἱ τὸ κάλλος κάθηται, καὶ τοῦτο οἶδε, καὶ ἐπ' αὐτῷ κομᾷ, καὶ σοβαρός ἐστι, καὶ θαῤῥεῖ τοῖς πτεροῖς, ἅπερ οὖν αὐτῷ καὶ κόσμον παρατίθησι, καὶ πρὸς τοὺς ἔξωθεν φόβον ἀποστέλλει. [Ho taōs oiden ornithōn hōraiotatos ōn, kai entha hoi to kallos kathētai, kai touto oide, kai ep' autō koma, kai sobaros esti, kai tharrei tois pterois, haper oun autō kai kosmon paratithēsi, kai pros tous exōthen phobon apostellei.] The peacock knows that he is the most beautiful of all birds, and he knows very well where his beauty lies, and prides himself on it, and is haughty, and trusts in his plumage, which both gives him adornment and strikes others with a kind of fear. And below: Ὅπως ἔχει τῆς εἰς τὴν ἐπίδειξιν ἀφθονίας παρίστησιν. ἐᾷ γὰρ ἐμπλησθῆναι τῆς θέας τὸν παρεστῶτα, καὶ ἑαυτὸν περιάγει, δεικνὺς φιλοπόνως τὸ τῆς πτερώσεως πολύμορφον. [Hopōs echei tēs eis tēn epideixin aphthonias paristēsin. ea gar emplēsthēnai tēs theas ton parestōta, kai heauton periagei, deiknys philoponōs to tēs pterōseōs polymorphon.] He shows how great a desire he has to display himself. For he lets the spectator take his fill of the sight of him, and turns himself in every direction, showing with great zeal the variety of his feathers. Especially in flowery, springtime meadows, as Lucian observes in On the Hall: Οὗτος, ἐκπετάσας τὰ πτερὰ, καὶ ἀναδείξας τῷ ἡλίῳ, καὶ τὴν οὐρὰν ἐπάρας, καὶ πάντοθεν αὐτῷ περιστήσας, ἐπιδείκνυται τὰ ἄνθη τὰ αὐτοῦ, καὶ τὸ ἔαρ τῶν πτερῶν, ὥσπερ αὐτὸν προκαλοῦντος τοῦ λειμῶνος ἐς τὴν ἅμιλλαν. [Houtos, ekpetasas ta ptera, kai anadeixas tō hēliō, kai tēn ouran eparas, kai pantothen autō peristēsas, epideiknytai ta anthē ta autou, kai to ear tōn pterōn, hōsper auton prokalountos tou leimōnos es tēn hamillan.] He, with his feathers spread out and shown to the sun, and his tail raised and expanded all around, displays his own flowers too, and the springtime of his feathers, as if he were challenged to this contest by the meadow. Thus in the first book of Achilles Tatius there is described in a garden ὁ ταὼς τοῖς ἄνθεσιν περισύρων τὸ πτερὸν [ho taōs tois anthesin perisyrōn to pteron], the peacock spreading his feathers around the flowers. But by this same art he also attracts the females. In the same place, a little below: Ὅταν ἐπαγαγέσθαι θέλῃ τὴν ἐρωμένην, τότε οὕτως καλλωπίζεται· [Hotan epagagesthai thelē tēn erōmenēn, tote houtōs kallōpizetai] When he wishes to attract the female he loves, then he adorns himself in this way. And of the peahen next to him: Ταύτῃ νῦν οὗτος τὸ κάλλος ἐπιδείκνυται, λειμῶνα πτερῶν· [Tautē nyn houtos to kallos epideiknytai, leimōna pterōn] To her he now displays his beauty, namely the [II, 842] meadow of his feathers. Hence Nazianzen, Oration 34: Ταῖς θηλείαις, ὥς φασι, καλλωπίζεται, τὸν αὐχένα διάρας, καὶ τὸ πτερὸν κυκλοτέρως, περιστήσας τὸ χρυσαυγὲς, καὶ κατάστερον, θεατρίζει τὸ κάλλος τοῖς ἐράσταις μετὰ σοβαροῦ τοῦ βαδίσματος. [Tais thēleiais, hōs phasi, kallōpizetai, ton auchena diaras, kai to pteron kykloterōs, peristēsas to chrysauges, kai katasteron, theatrizei to kallos tois erastais meta sobarou tou badismatos.] He shows himself off, as they say, to his females; and, with neck raised and his feathers, which reflect the gleam of gold and stars, arranged in a circle, he sets forth his beauty for his lovers to view, as in a theatre, with a kind of proud gait. In the same way Eustathius in the Hexaëmeron: Τῶν πτερῶν ἐπιδείξας τὸ θέατρον ἐπάγεται πρὸς συνουσίαν τὴν θήλειαν, ὥσπερ λειμῶνα τὸν καλλωπισμὸν τοῦτον ἐπιδεικνὺς αὐτῇ. [Tōn pterōn epideixas to theatron epagetai pros synousian tēn thēleian, hōsper leimōna ton kallōpismon touton epideiknys autē.] Displaying the theatre of his feathers he entices the female to mating, exhibiting this adornment to her like a meadow. For more on the same theme see the Iambics of Philes [=Manuel Philes, De animalium proprietate (14th c.)] on the peacock, which begin thus:
Πτεροῖς ὁ ταὼς γαυριῶν πολυχρόοις, [Pterois ho taōs gauriōn polychroois,]

The peacock, proud of its many-coloured feathers, etc. And among the Grammarians, who hold that ταὼν [taōn] is so called ἀπὸ τῆς τάσεως [apo tēs taseōs], from extension, or παρὰ τὸ τείνειν τὴν οὐράν· τὸ γὰρ ζῶον ἐναβρυνόμενον τῷ ἑαυτοῦ κάλλει τοῖς ὁρῶσι τὴν οὐρὰν ἑξαπλοῦν ἀποδεικνύει [para to teinein tēn ouran; to gar zōon enabrynomenon tō heautou kallei tois horōsi tēn ouran hexaploun apodeiknyei], because it spreads out its tail; for this animal, proud of its beauty, displays its sixfold tail to the onlookers. And in Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān] too the Arabs say that it is in its nature حب الزهو بنفسه والخيلا والاعجاب بريشه وعقد ذنبه كالطاقة اذا كانت الانثي ناظرة اليه [ḥubb al-zahw bi-nafsihi wa-l-khuyalāʾ wa-l-iʿjāb bi-rīshihi wa-ʿaqd dhanabihi ka-l-ṭāqa idhā kānat al-unthá nāẓiratan ilayhi] that it loves to gaze upon itself with vainglory and pride, and admires its feathers, and arranges its tail into a circle when the female looks at it.

Yet no one should hope that it can be concluded from this that in the words of Job רננים renanim are peacocks. For many reasons stand against it. The first [col. 242] is taken from history, both sacred and profane. For both teach that the peacock was first brought from India, long after the times of Job. In sacred history this is found in 1 Reg. X, 22. and 2 Chr 9:21: Once in three years the fleet (of Solomon) came from Tarshish, bringing gold and silver, elephants' teeth, apes, ותכיים, and peacocks. None of the ancients renders the Hebrew word otherwise, as we said in its place ^{b)}. Moreover, there would have been no need to bring peacocks into Judaea from such distant regions if the Jews, or the Arabs neighbouring the Jews, had already had them long before. Now, if we consult the Greeks, Theophrastus, as cited by Pliny, reports that peacocks are imported into Asia. And Aelian, History of Animals, book 5, chapter 21: Λέγεται δὲ ἐκ βαρβάρων εἰς Ἕλληνας κομισθῆναι· καὶ χρόνου πολλοῦ σπάνιος ὢν, εἶτα ἐδείκνυτο τῶν ἀνθρώπων τοῖς φιλοκάλοις μισθοῦ. Καὶ Ἀθήνησί γε ταῖς [II, 843] νουμηνίαις ἐδέχοντο καὶ ἄνδρας, καὶ γυναῖκας, ἐπὶ τὴν ἱστορίαν αὐτῶν, καὶ τὴν θέαν πρόσοδον εἶχον. ἐτιμῶντο δὲ τὸν ἄῤῥενα, καὶ τὴν θῆλυν δραχμῶν χιλίων· ὡς Ἀντιφῶν ἐν τῷ Πρὸς Ἐρασίστρατον λόγῳ φησί. [Legetai de ek barbarōn eis Hellēnas komisthēnai; kai chronou pollou spanios ōn, eita edeiknyto tōn anthrōpōn tois philokalois misthou. Kai Athēnēsi ge tais noumēniais edechonto kai andras, kai gynaikas, epi tēn historian autōn, kai tēn thean prosodon eichon. etimōnto de ton arrena, kai tēn thēlyn drachmōn chiliōn; hōs Antiphōn en tō Pros Erasistraton logō phēsi.] It is said to have been brought from the barbarians to the Greeks; and since it was for a long time rare, it was at last shown to the curious for a fixed fee. And at Athens, when men and women were admitted to see it on the first day of the month, they made a profit from it. And they valued a male and female at a thousand drachmas, as Antiphon says in the Speech Against Erasistratus. This speech had another title, Περὶ ταῶν [Peri taōn], On Peacocks, as we learn from Athenaeus, book 9, chapter 12. But that title seems to have been added by someone else, for the author himself calls them nothing but ὄρνεις ποικίλους [orneis poikilous], variegated birds. Was it perhaps because the name ταῶν [taōn], then recent, he did not yet dare to use in a speech? Indeed ταὼς [taōs] is read in the Birds of Aristophanes, and in the Acharnians, Τοῖς ταῶσι [Tois taōsi]. But, besides the fact that Aristophanes was somewhat later than Antiphon, the rules of oratory and of comedy are different: comedy uses the words of the common people, oratory a polished and more correct style. However that may be, we learn from the same speech that peacocks had begun to be kept at Athens thirty years earlier, in the house of a certain Demus, son of Pyrilampes, καὶ πολλοὺς παραγίνεσθαι μετὰ πόθον τῆς τῶν ὀρνίθων θέας ἔκ τε Λακεδαίμονος, καὶ Θετταλίας [kai pollous paraginesthai meta pothon tēs tōn ornithōn theas ek te Lakedaimonos, kai Thettalias], and that many came (to Athens) from Lacedaemon and Thessaly out of desire to see these birds. From which you may infer that these birds then first began to become known to the Greeks. Nor can the age of Pyrilampes be uncertain, since Plutarch in the Pericles relates that he was a friend of Pericles, and even mentions his τὰς ὀρνιθοτροφίας, καὶ ταῶνας [tas ornithotrophias, kai taōnas], aviaries and peacocks. Accordingly, in the age of Alexander there were still few peacocks in Greece. And, on the testimony of Aelian, in the place cited above, Ἀλέξανδρος ὁ Μακεδὼν ἐν Ἰνδοῖς ἰδὼν τούσδε τοὺς ὀρνίθας ἐξεπλάγη, καὶ τοῦ κάλλους θαυμάσας ἠπείλησε τῷ καταθύσαντι ταὼν ἀπειλὰς βαρυτάτας· [Alexandros ho Makedōn en Indois idōn tousde tous ornithas exeplagē, kai tou kallous thaumasas ēpeilēse tō katathysanti taōn apeilas barytatas;] Alexander the Macedonian, seeing these birds among the Indians, was struck with admiration for their beauty and threatened the severest penalties on anyone who killed a peacock. Curtius too, in book 9, testifies that Alexander found wild peacocks near the Indian river Hydraotes: From here, he says, they came through deserts to the river Hydraotes. Adjoining the river was a grove shady with trees unknown elsewhere, and full of a multitude of wild peacocks. From this very passage one learns that the peacock came from India. Hence the same Aelian, as above, book 11, chapter 33: Ταὼν δὲ Ἰνδικὸν δῶρον λαβὼν ὁ τῶν Αἰγυπτίων βασιλεὺς ταὼν, ὡς ἰδεῖν, μέγιστόν τε καὶ ὡραιότατον· [Taōn de Indikon dōron labōn ho tōn Aigyptiōn basileus taōn, hōs idein, megiston te kai hōraiotaton;] When the king of Egypt had received as a gift an Indian peacock, a very large and very beautiful one. And book 13, chapter 18, where he describes the palace of the king of the Indians: Ἐν δὲ τοῖς παραδείσοις τρέφονται μὲν ταὼς ἥμεροι· [En de tois paradeisois trephontai men taōs hēmeroi;] In his gardens tame peacocks are kept. And book 16, ch. 2: Γίνονται δὲ καὶ ταὼς ἐν Ἰνδοῖς τῶν πανταχόθι μέγιστοι. [Ginontai de kai taōs en Indois tōn pantachothi megistoi.] There are also in India by far the largest peacocks. And Lucian in the Ship: Ὄρνις ἐκ Φάσιδος, καὶ ταὼς ἐξ Ἰνδίας. [Ornis ek Phasidos, kai taōs ex Indias.] A fowl from the Phasis (the pheasant), and a peacock from India. [II, 844] Therefore, when Menodotus of Samos writes of peacocks, Πρώτιστοι καὶ ἐγένοντο, καὶ ἐτράφησαν ἐν Σάμῳ, καὶ ἐντεῦθεν εἰς τοὺς ἔξω τόπους διεδόθησαν, ὡς καὶ οἱ ἀλεκτρυόνες ἐν τῇ Περσίδι, καὶ αἱ καλούμεναι μελεαγρίδες ἐν τῇ Αἰτωλίᾳ· [col. 243] [Prōtistoi kai egenonto, kai etraphēsan en Samō, kai enteuthen eis tous exō topous diedothēsan, hōs kai hoi alektryones en tē Perside, kai hai kaloumenai meleagrides en tē Aitōlia;] They were first born and reared in Samos, and from there spread into other regions, as cocks from Persia, and the so-called guinea fowl from Aetolia: there is no doubt that he lies to flatter his own people. And it is objected in vain that there is an ancient fable about Argus, killed by Mercury and changed into a peacock. For the history or fable that ascribes the slaying of Argus to Mercury must be very ancient, since from it Mercury is called Ἀργειφόντης [Argeiphontēs] by Homer and Hesiod; but the metamorphosis of Argus into a peacock is a recent invention, and I find no author of it older than Moschus. Thus Apollodorus, roughly contemporary with Moschus, in book 2 of the Library, relates the slaying of Argus by Mercury without a γρῦ [gry] about his metamorphosis; nor does the old Scholiast of Homer on Iliad β′ [2] at the word Ἀργειφόντης [Argeiphontēs]. From this it appears that this fable was new and not widely accepted. Yet from it, once it arose, peacocks at last began to be regarded as the bird of Juno, to be attached by the poets to the goddess's chariot, to be kept in her temple at Samos, and even to be struck on the coins of the Samians, which survive to this day. I am not unaware that the Scholiast of Aristophanes holds that this fable is alluded to when, in the Birds, Euelpides says to the Hoopoe,
Τηρεὺς γὰρ εἶ σύ; πότερον ὄρνις, ἢ ταώς; [Tēreus gar ei sy? poteron ornis, ē taōs?]

The Epops, namely, had said that he had been Tereus, because Tereus is fabled to have been changed into an ἔποπα [epopa], or upupa [hoopoe]. The Scholiast therefore conjectures that by the name of Tereus Euelpides meant Argus, who was called Τηρεὺς [Tēreus] παρὰ τὸ τηρεῖν τὴν Ἰὼ [para to tērein tēn Iō], and so asked whether he was a peacock, according to the fable which says that Argus was changed into a peacock. But this conjecture is colder than a Gallic winter. Here an allusion to the fable of Argus is sought in vain: Euelpides merely doubts whether the Epops was presenting himself as a hoopoe or as a peacock, because the mark he had assumed in order to be taken for a hoopoe, that is, a crest of feathers, also suits the peacock. Peacocks, however, once so rare in Greece, at length began to be cheap. This is shown by these lines of Antiphanes, a most celebrated poet of Middle Comedy:

Τῶν ταῶν μὲν ὡς ἅπαξ τις ζεῦγος ἤγαγεν μόνον, Σπάνιον ὂν τὸ χρῆμα· πλείους δ᾽ εἰσὶ νῦν τῶν ὀρτύγων. [Tōn taōn men hōs hapax tis zeugos ēgagen monon, spanion on to chrēma; pleious d' eisi nyn tōn ortygōn.]

Once someone brought in just a single pair of peacocks, then a rare bird; but now they are more numerous than quails. The very same happened at Rome, where Hortensius ^{c)} was the first to kill a peacock for food at Rome, at the inaugural banquet of his priesthood. M. Aufidius Lurco was the first to introduce their fattening, around the time of the last war against the pirates, and from [II, 845] that trade he drew an income of sixty thousand sesterces. Against this luxury of the gluttons of his age Publius Syrus inveighs thus in Petronius:
In the gaping maw of luxury the walls of Mars grow slack ^{d)}: For your palate the peacock is kept penned and fed, Clad in its golden Babylonian plumage.

For many, following Hortensius, as Varro testifies in book 3, chapter 6 of his Rustica, raised the prices of peacocks: So that, he says, their eggs sell for five denarii each, and the birds themselves easily for fifty. At these words of Varro Macrobius (Saturnal. book 3, ch. 13) exclaims thus: Behold a thing not only to be wondered at, but to be ashamed of: that peacocks' eggs should sell for five denarii, which today, I will not say sell more cheaply, but do not sell at all! From this it is gathered that the peacock was a foreign bird both at Rome and in Greece. The true homeland of peacocks is of course in India, as we have proved. From there I should think they were first carried over into Persia, Media, and Babylonia; and hence they are called Median and Persian, and are attributed to Babylonia, as we have shown in its place ^{e)}. They were also brought into Judaea under the reign of Solomon, and into Greece not long before Alexander. From there they gradually spread to Rome and the other parts of the West. Since, then, in Job's time India was inaccessible, it is hardly likely that the peacock was known to him or to the Arabs of his age. If anyone replies that it is God who speaks there, to whom all things are known, he will achieve nothing. For God did not prove his power [col. 244] or providence to Job from things unknown to him. 2. Moreover, if the peacock were treated here, a bird so exceptional and something of a marvel, so great a subject would not be dispatched in so few words and so cursorily; nor, in a chapter in which lions, ibexes, wild asses, horses, ostriches, eagles, etc. are each described in many verses, would it be said of the peacock alone, The peacock exults with its wings. And reason scarcely allows the descriptions of the peacock and the ostrich to be joined in the same verse. 3. Why would peacocks be called רננים renanim from their song, when they have an utterly harsh and uncouth voice, which is therefore called a screech by Palladius? ^{f)} So in Phaedrus book 3, fable 57, the peacock complains to Juno that he is laughed at as soon as he utters his voice. 4. The only argument brought forward to prove that the רננים renanim are peacocks, namely that they are said to exult with their wings, proves exactly the contrary, and can be turned forcibly back against those who hold this view. For it is not characteristic of peacocks to exult with their wings, but with their tail. For there lie the jewels by whose splendour it displays itself. Lucretius, book 2:
And the peacock's tail, when it is filled with abundant light, Changes its colours in like manner as it is turned. [II, 846] Ovid, book 15 of the Metamorphoses, fable 35:
Juno's bird, which bears stars on its tail.
Statius, book 2 of the Silvae, in Melior's Parrot:
Whom the Junonian bird with its jewelled tail could not surpass in appearance. —
The Epigrams of the ancients, where on Gentia and Choë:
When the Junonian bird shakes and spreads its tail, It gracefully bears a thousand eyes, a thousand jewels.

Chrysippus admires this so much that he asserts τὸ ζῶον γεγονέναι ἕνεκα τῆς κέρκου, καὶ οὐκ ἀνάπαλιν [to zōon gegonenai heneka tēs kerkou, kai ouk anapalin], that this animal was created for the sake of its tail, and not the reverse, that is, the tail for the sake of the animal. So Plutarch in the book De Stoicorum contrar. Accordingly, to show itself off, it spreads not its wings but its tail. Pliny: At the same time it seeks with its tail curved like a shell certain reflections of shade for the other feathers, which gleam more brightly in the dark. Columella: It covers itself, as if admiring itself, with the jewelled feathers of its tail. Dio Chrysostom: Ἀνακλάσας ^{g)} τὴν οὐρὰν, καὶ περιστήσας αὐτῷ πανταχόθεν ὥσπερ εὐειδὲς θέατρον [Anaklasas tēn ouran, kai peristēsas autō pantachothen hōsper eueides theatron]. Bending back its tail, and setting it up all around itself like a handsome theatre. Phaedrus, book 3, Fable 57:
And unfolding its jewelled tail with painted plumage.

Lucian: Τὴν οὐρὰν ἐπάρας, καὶ πάντοθεν αὐτῷ περιστήσας, ἐπιδείκνυται τὰ ἄνθη τὰ αὐτοῦ [Tēn ouran eparas, kai pantothen autō peristēsas, epideiknytai ta anthē ta autou]; With its tail raised and spread all around, it also displays its flowers. The Etymologicum: Τοῖς ὁρῶσι τὴν οὐρὰν ἑξαπλοῦν ἀποδεικνύει [Tois horōsi tēn ouran hexaploun apodeiknyei]. It displays its sixfold tail to the onlookers. Damir: عقد ذنبه كالطاقة [ʿaqada dhanabahu ka-l-ṭāqa] It arranges its tail like an arched work. Hence it is that with the tail the peacock's whole glory perishes. Pliny: Therefore, when its tail is lost each year together with the leaves of the trees, until it grows again with the blossom, it seeks a hiding place, ashamed and mournful. I am not unaware that the poets attribute to the wings, καταχρηστικῶς [katachrēstikōs], what belongs properly to the tail. Moschus:
Ὄρνις ἀγαλλόμενος πτερύγων πολυανθέϊ χροίῃ, [Ornis agallomenos pterygōn polyanthei chroiē,]
A bird exulting in the flowery colour of its wings. Martial in the Xenia, Epigram 70:
You marvel whenever it unfolds its jewelled wings.
Claudian, Against Rufinus, book 1:

The patrician fans himself with rosy peacocks' wings. [II, 847] With peacocks' wings, that is, tails. For fans of this kind were made from the peacock's tail. Martial in the Apophoreta, on a peacock fly-whisk:
That which keeps the foul flies from licking your meal was the proud tail of a splendid bird.
Propertius, book 2, the Elegy to Demophoon:
And now fans from the proud peacock's tail.

But in Scripture כנף, in a bird, signifies nothing other than the wing. Therefore רננים [col. 245] renanim must be birds that truly exult in their wings, or that have in their wings some ground for exulting.

That these are ostriches, many things not only suggest but prove. 1. The authority of Jerome, who rendered it so; no such authority is brought forward by those who understand peacocks here. 2. Just as the two verbs ענה ana and רנן ranan are entirely synonymous in the sense of crying out and singing, so it is credible that the two bird names derived from them, which are moreover of almost the same form, are synonymous: namely יענים jeenim and רננים renanim. Therefore, as יענים means female ostriches, as we proved above ^{b)}, so too does רננים. These, moreover, are so named διακριτικῶς [diakritikōs], because, while the voice of the male is deeper and harsher, the voice of the female is more melodious. Accordingly of the male they say عار [ʿār] arra, but of the female زمر [zamara] zamara, which is to sing. And the female's voice itself is called زمار [zimār] zimar, or song. 3. Ostriches are rightly said to exult in their wings, since their swiftness depends wholly on their wings: for although these are useless to them for flight, yet they help them wonderfully in running, and are like sails on a ship. This ancient and modern writers report by common consent. Xenophon, Anabasis (Cyrus the Younger), book 1: Στρουθὸν δὲ οὐδεὶς ἔλαβεν, etc. Πολὺ γὰρ ἀπέσπα ὑποφεύγουσα, τοῖς μὲν ποσὶ δρόμῳ, ταῖς δὲ πτέρυξιν ἄρασα, ὥσπερ ἱστίῳ χρωμένη [Strouthon de oudeis elaben, etc. Poly gar apespa hypopheugousa, tois men posi dromō, tais de pteryxin arasa, hōsper histiō chrōmenē]. No one caught an ostrich, etc. For in flight it drew far away, running with its feet, but raised by its wings and using them as a sail. Diodorus, book 3: Ὅταν κατ᾽ ἀνέμου πνοὰς ἐξαίρῃ τὰς πτέρυγας ὑπερεξάγει καθαπερεί τις ναῦς ἱστιοδρομοῦσα [Hotan kat᾽ anemou pnoas exairē tas pterygas hyperexagei kathaperei tis naus histiodromousa]; When it raises its wings with a following wind, it is carried like a ship under full sail. And shortly after: Ὅταν δὲ ἐν νηνεμίᾳ διώκηται, ταχὺ συνιδρουσῶν τοῦ πτερύγων ἀδυνατεῖ χρήσασθαι τοῖς τῆς φύσεως προτηρήμασιν, καὶ ῥᾳδίως καταλαμβανόμενον ἁλίσκεται [Hotan de en nēnemia diōkētai, tachy synidrousōn tou pterygōn adynatei chrēsasthai tois tēs physeōs protērēmasin, kai rhadiōs katalambanomenon haliksetai]; But when they pursue the animal in a calm, its wings soon become soaked with sweat, and since it cannot use its natural defences, they overtake it without any trouble and catch it. Aelian, book 2, chapter 27: Ἡ στρουθὸς ἡ μεγάλη λασίοις μὲν τοῖς πτεροῖς ἐπτέρωται [Hē strouthos hē megalē lasiois men tois pterois epterōtai].

[II, 848] ἀρθῆναι δὲ, καὶ εἰς βαθὺν ἀέρα μετεωρισθῆναι φύσιν οὐκ ἔχει. θεῖ δὲ ὤκιστα, καὶ τὰς παρὰ τὴν πλευρὰν ἑκατέραν πτέρυγας ἁπλοῖ, καὶ ἐμπῖπτον τὸ πνεῦμα κολποῖ, δίκην ἱστίων αὐτάς. [arthēnai de, kai eis bathyn aera meteōristhēnai physin ouk echei. thei de ōkista, kai tas para tēn pleuran hekateran pterygas haploi, kai empipton to pneuma kolpoi, dikēn histiōn autas.] The ostrich is indeed furnished with dense wings. Yet its nature does not allow it to be lifted from the ground by them and borne aloft. But it runs as swiftly as possible and spreads out its wings on either side, and the wind fills them like sails. And in book 4, chapter 37: Εἰ δὲ αὐτὴν διώκοι τις, ἥδε οὐκ ἐπιτολμᾷ τῇ πτήσει, θεῖ δὲ τὰς πτέρυγας ἁπλώσασα· [Ei de autēn diōkoi tis, hēde ouk epitolma tē ptēsei, thei de tas pterygas haplōsasa;] If anyone pursues it, it does not attempt to fly, but runs with its wings spread out. And in book 8, chapter 10, the same author relates that elephants in battle spread out their wide ears δίκην τῶν στρουθῶν τῶν μεγάλων, ἅπερ οὖν τὰς πτέρυγας ἁπλώσασαι, ἢ φεύγουσιν, ἢ ἐπιᾶσιν [dikēn tōn strouthōn tōn megalōn, haper oun tas pterygas haplōsasai, ē pheugousin, ē epiasin], in the manner of ostriches, which, whether they flee or attack, move with wings spread out. Philes, chapter 3:
Κολποῦν ἑαυτῆς τὰ πτερὰ πρὸς τὸν δρόμον, ῾Ως λαῖφος οἰδοῦν ἐκ πνοῆς πλησιστίου· [Kolpoun heautēs ta ptera pros ton dromon, Hōs laiphos oidoun ek pnoēs plēsistiou;]

Spreading its wings for running, like a sail swelling with the wind that fills it. Hence Pliny, book 10, chapter 20: they surpass the speed (of a horseman), their wings having been given them only for this, to help them as they run. And Claudian, Against Eutropius, book 2:
As the huge bird of Libya, when pressed by the cries of hunters, crosses the hot sands at a run, and, its wings curved by the blast like a sail, flies amid the dust. —

He says both run and fly, because the gait of the ostrich in flight is something between running and flying, or a mixture of the two. To this belong these words of Plautus in the Persa, Act 2, Scene 2:
Fly at a run. P. That is what the sea-sparrow usually does around the circus. [col. 246]

Sea sparrow, that is, ostrich. Nor do more recent writers describe the ostrich's running to us otherwise. Leo Africanus, book 9: It has large black feathers in its wings, by which, though useless for flight, it is helped in running through frequent movement of the wings and tail. You may read the same in Marmol, Africa, book 1, chapter 23. So among the Arabs Alkazuinius [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt]: اذا عدت النعامة ارخت جناحيها الي رجليها فلا يسبقها شي من الحيوانات [idhā ʿadat al-naʿāma arkhat janāḥayhā ilā rijlayhā fa-lā yasbiquhā shayʾ min al-ḥayawānāt] When the ostrich runs, it lets its wings down as far as its feet, and no animal overtakes it. But in the same place a thing utterly false is related: اذا استقبلت الريح كان اشد ما اذا استدبرتها [idhā istaqbalat al-rīḥ kāna ashadd mā idhā istadbarathā] When it has the wind against it, it runs more vigorously than when it has it behind. This is contrary both to nature and to the testimonies of the ancients [II, 849]. So Abu Ubeid in the same place wears himself out in vain searching for the cause of this marvel. I cannot but add a proverb of the Arabs in Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī]: ركب جناحي النعامة [rakiba janāḥay al-naʿāma] He rode the wings of the ostrich, that is, جد في الامر واجتهد [jadda fī al-amr wa-ijtahada] He did something with great zeal and diligence. Damir explains the same proverb at much greater length. But let it suffice to have shown from this that, in the opinion of the Arabs, nothing is swifter than the wings of ostriches. Exultation can also be attributed to the wings of ostriches in another sense. Cardano, book 10 De subtilitate: No bird has such charm or beauty in its feathers; for this reason soldiers adorn their helmets with no others. This was already the custom long ago. Theophrastus, Historia plantarum, book 4, chapter 5, on a certain Indian tree: Τὸ φύλλον τὴν μὲν μορφὴν πρόμηκες, τοῖς τῶν στρουθῶν πτεροῖς ὅμοιον, ἃ παρατίθενται παρὰ τὰ κράνη· [To phyllon tēn men morphēn promēkes, tois tōn strouthōn pterois homoion, ha paratithentai para ta kranē] The leaf, oblong in shape, like the plumes of ostriches which are put on helmets. Pliny, in the place cited above: And feathers adorning war crests and helmets. These feathers, moreover, are taken from the wings as well as from the tail. Nor is there any animal whose feathers are so even; accordingly we read that among the Egyptians the ostrich feather was the symbol of equity. Horus, book 2, near the end: Ἄνθρωπον ἴσως τὸ δίκαιον ἀπονέμοντα βουλόμενοι σημῆναι, στρουθοκαμήλου πτερὸν γράφουσι· τοῦτο γὰρ τὸ ζῶον πανταχόθεν ἴσα ἔχει τὰ πτερυγώματα παρὰ τῶν ἄλλων. [Anthrōpon isōs to dikaion aponemonta boulomenoi sēmēnai, strouthokamēlou pteron graphousi; touto gar to zōon pantachothen isa echei ta pterygōmata para tōn allōn.] Wishing to signify a man who distributes justice equally to all, they paint an ostrich feather: for this animal, beyond the rest, has the feathers of its wings equal on every side. This very thing adds grace and beauty to the wings of ostriches. 4. Besides the ostrich, the Sacred Writer describes ten animals in this and the following chapter, and the names of all of them are read, as a heading, right in the first hemistich. Thus he begins the description of the lion: Will you hunt the prey for the lioness? And when he passes from there to the raven: Who provided food for the raven? Then, coming to the ibexes, he says: Do you know when the ibexes of the rocks give birth? And afterwards of the wild ass: Who let the wild ass go free? And of the rim, which the interpreters take to be the unicorn: Will the rim be willing to serve you? Why then, by the same reasoning, should not the ostrich also be placed in the first part of the verse? Especially since the descriptions that follow, of the horse, the hawk, the eagle, and of Behemoth and Leviathan, always keep the same rule. Here, then, I shall believe the matter stands in the same way, and that in the first part of the verse is read the name of the animal whose vivid description follows, until someone produces a reason for a difference, and here none presents itself. 5. Since it is agreed that the following description pertains to the [col. 247] ostrich, its name had to be put first, just as with the ten other animals which are described by Job. But if רננים renanim are not ostriches, it is certain that the name of the ostrich appears nowhere in this verse. For it is certain that חסידה chasida, which they explain as ostrich, is not the ostrich; since it is a migratory bird, Ierem. VIII, 7, and flies aloft, [II, 850] Zech 5:9, and nests in fir trees, Ps 104:17, and has its name from piety: חסידה chasida literally means pious. This name in no way suits the ostrich, since in Lam 4:3 and in this very passage the ostrich is described as a bird impious and pitiless towards its young. Unless they would have it called חסידה κατ᾽ ἀντίφρασιν [kat᾽ antiphrasin], in the way, namely, that they call the Furies Eumenides. Therefore the best interpreters, and even those very ones who would have chasida here be the ostrich, consistently render it elsewhere as stork. That this rendering is most true I shall prove at length in its place. Among the recent interpreters there is one learned and pious man to whom these things were by no means unknown. He, then, although carried away by the common error he takes רננים renanim for peacocks, nevertheless explains חסידה chasida as stork. But because the name of the ostrich could not be absent from this verse without sacrilege, he would have the last word נוצה be not only a bird, with R. Selomo, but the ostrich. But if נוצה is the name of a bird, since it is formed from flying (for the verb נצה means to fly), it will not fit the ostrich, which alone of birds lacks flight and never raises itself from the ground. What of the fact that נוצה is not even a bird? For נוצה signifies nothing other than feather or plumage. This is clear from Ezek 17:3, where the eagle is described as מלא הנוצה, full of plumage, and רב נוצה, of much plumage, or abounding in plumage, as he himself renders it. Why then should a word which there means plumage be taken here for a bird, and indeed for the ostrich? Why should a new and unheard-of meaning be attached to this word, without witness, without example, without any shadow of reason, a meaning which the very origin of the word plainly refutes? From this it follows that the ostrich is not named in the last hemistich, and must therefore be sought in the first, namely in the word רננים renanim. Otherwise it would be entirely absent from this verse ^{R1}. And when it is said in the verse immediately following, She leaves her eggs on the ground, etc. (which it is certain are said of the ostrich), these things would be said [II, 851] of a bird that has nowhere been named before, and the discourse would be left hanging, nor would these words cohere in any way with what precedes.

With these preliminaries, we shall now try to interpret the whole verse. In Hebrew it reads thus: כנף רננים נעלסה אם אברה חסידה ונוצה, which we render word for word as follows: The wing of the ostriches exults, truly the wing of the stork, and the plumage: that is, which is truly a wing and plumage such as in the stork. The particle אם im is mostly the same as IF, or is a mark of interrogation, like WHETHER, ἄρα [ara], πότερον [poteron]; but also, as Kimchi points out, ויש שהוא כמו האמת. It also occurs for TRULY, and is a particle of affirmation, as if formed from אמן, amen, with the Nun dropped, as in אמת for אמנת ^{R2}. Examples of this meaning are found at Gen 47:18. Num 16:30. Job 22:20. Ps 59:16 and LXIII, 7. Prov 3:34 and XXIII, 18. Isa 4:4 and XXIX, 16. etc. The wing of the stork, אברה חסידה, for אברת חסידה: the absolute state for the construct, which is not without examples. Thus Deut 16:21. אשרה כל עץ, a grove of any tree, for אשרת. Ruth 2:17. איפה שערים, an ephah of barley, for איפת. 2 Reg. VII, 1. סאה סולת, a seah of fine flour, for סאת. Ps 45:5. וענוה צדק, and of the meekness of righteousness, for וענות. Isa 24:22. אספה אסיר, with the gathering of a prisoner, for אספת. Isa 42:25. חמה אפו, the heat of his anger, for חמת. These Kimchi in his Commentaries repeatedly explains by ellipsis, as if one said אשרה אשרת כל עץ, a grove, a grove, I say, of any tree: [col. 248] as when we read at Exod 38:21. אלה פקודי המשכן משכן העדה, These are the things numbered of the tabernacle, of the tabernacle of the testimony. And Num 32:1. המקום מקום מקנה, the place, a place of cattle. And Ps 133:2. על הזקן זקן אהרן, upon the beard, the beard of Aaron. And Ezek 47:3. במים מי אפסים, in the waters, waters of the ankles. So in the passage we are dealing with, if the expression were complete, it would read אברה אברת חסידה, a wing, a wing, I say, of the stork: or, if you prefer, one may supply כף דמיון, the Caph of similitude, so that אברה חסידה stands for אברה כחסידה, a wing like that of the stork. Expressions of this kind occur everywhere. As Gen 49:9. Judah, a lion's whelp. And Deut 33:22. Dan, a lion's whelp, that is, like a lion's whelp. Gen 49:14. Issachar, a strong ass, that is, like an ass. Deut 28:23 Your heavens bronze, the earth iron, that is, like bronze, like iron. 2 Sam 1:21. The shield of Saul not anointed, that is, as if not anointed. Job 7:9 The cloud has vanished and gone, so he who goes down to the grave, etc. Has vanished [II, 852] כלה, for ככלה, as it vanished. Job 11:12 Man is born a wild ass, that is, like a wild ass. Ps 11:1 How do you say to my soul, that it should flee from your mountain צפור, a bird, that is, כצפור, like a bird. Ps 14:4 Eating my people, they eat bread, that is, as they eat bread. Ps 119:119 You have removed all the wicked of the earth as dross, that is, like dross. Proverb. XVII, 22. A merry heart ייטב גהה, does good, a medicine, that is, כגהה, like a medicine. Song 1:15 Your eyes doves', that is, like doves'. Can. VII, 5. Your eyes the pools in Heshbon, for like the pools. Lam 4:7 Their polish sapphires, that is, like sapphires. Mic 3:12. Zion shall be ploughed a field, for like a field.

So much for the words. As for the sense, we have already explained the first hemistich fully and shown in what sense the wing of ostriches is said to exult, or to be glad. But concerning the second hemistich, truly the wing of the stork, and plumage, or truly a wing as of a stork, and plumage, two questions can be asked. 1. What is the point of that affirmation, TRULY a wing, and plumage? 2. Why is it called the wing and plumage of a stork, or as of a stork? To the first I answer that the ostrich is a bird that is not a bird, which in many respects approaches the nature of a quadruped. This was long ago observed by the Philosopher in book 4 of On the Parts, near the end. His words are: It has some features proper to a bird and some proper to a quadruped. That it is not a quadruped is suggested by its having feathers; that it is not a bird, by its not flying aloft and having feathers not suited to flight but hair-like. Moreover, like a quadruped it has upper eyelashes, and it is bare on the head and on the upper part of the neck, so that its eyelashes are rather hairy. But, like a bird, its lower parts are covered with plumage. And it is two-footed like a bird, but cloven-hoofed like a quadruped. For it does not have toes but a divided hoof; the cause of this is its size, which is not that of a bird but of a quadruped. Hence Diodorus, on Arabia, in book 2: Φέρει δὲ καὶ ζῶα διφυῆ, καὶ μεμιγμένα ταῖς ἰδέαις, ὧν αἱ μὲν ὀνομαζόμεναι στρουθοκάμηλοι περιειλήφασι τοῖς τύποις μίγματα χηνῶν, καὶ καμήλων· [Pherei de kai zōa diphyē, kai memigmena tais ideais, hōn hai men onomazomenai strouthokamēloi perieilēphasi tois typois migmata chēnōn, kai kamēlōn] It also produces animals of a double nature and of two forms, among which those called ostriches have an appearance mixed of geese and camels. For χηνῶν [chēnōn] read πτηνῶν [ptēnōn], because, having proved this part by part, he concludes that the ostrich χερσαῖον ἅμα φαίνεσθαι, καὶ πτηνὸν [chersaion hama phainesthai, kai ptēnon], seems at once a land animal and a winged one. Hence Herodotus calls them στρουθὸς καταγαίους [strouthous katagaious], that is, ground sparrows. And Pliny writes that they are almost of the genus of beasts. And Tertullian: A beast of some kind rather than a bird. And Alkazuinius: حيوان مركب من خلقة الطير والجمل [ḥayawān murakkab min khilqat al-ṭayr wa-l-jamal] It is an animal composed of the nature of a bird and of a camel. Hence there is a proverb of the Arabs in Damir, about one [col. 249] who is inconsistent and does not distinguish good from bad: النعامة لا طير ولا جمل [al-naʿāma lā ṭayr wa-lā jamal] The ostrich is neither bird nor camel. Accordingly, in Fable 28 of Gabrias [II, 853], when the wild beasts and the birds were disputing with each other, Λίβυσσα στρουθὸς [Libyssa strouthos], the Libyan ostrich, deceived both sides, since it seemed
Εἶναι μὲν ὄρνις, ἐκ μέρους δὲ θηρίον, Πτηνοῖς κάραν δεικνύσα, τοῖς θερσὶ πόδας, [Einai men ornis, ek merous de thērion, Ptēnois karan deiknysa, tois thersi podas,]

To be a bird indeed, but in part a wild beast, showing its head to the birds and its feet to the beasts. Since, then, this animal has so much of the quadruped, it is described here by the sacred writer together with the wild quadrupeds. And because it might seem a παράδοξος [paradoxos] thing that such an animal should have feathers and plumage like true birds, it is therefore set forth with this affirmation: Truly a wing, etc., and plumage; supply they have. Nor is it obscure why it is said to have not only feathers but the feathers of a stork. In the colour of its feathers the ostrich plainly resembles the stork. Marmol, in the place cited above: En las alas y en la cola tiene grandes plumas negras y blancas, come las de la cigueña. In its wings and tail it has large feathers, black and white, like the feathers of the stork. Hence Scaliger [=J. C. Scaliger, Exercitationes (1557)] ^{i)}, criticizing Cardano for attributing to the ostrich blue, white, black, red and green feathers, with which soldiers' helmets are adorned, says: The colours provoke laughter which you have transferred from the dyers' workshops into the storehouses of nature. For who would not laugh at you, peddling the claim that these colours which they fix on helmets are native to ostriches? For all are marked with dusky and white, as many African merchants told me. That I might understand it better, they compared it to the colour of the stork. This verse, thus explained, will shed light on those that follow ^{R3}.

notes.text: This very thing, however, seems probable to REISKE in his Conjecturis in Iobum et Proverbia Salomonis, Leipzig 1779, p. 162, who cannot persuade himself that רננים is a name of the ostrich. His words are: "But there is no great need for that name to be expressed. For it is the custom of the Arabs to discourse at length on some thing and yet not to name it. Asked why they do so, they answer, لعلم السمع بها [li-ʿilm al-samʿ bihā], because the hearer knows it, since the hearer, and hence also the reader, can very easily grasp from the character of the epithets, the predicates and the description, and from the whole thread of the discourse, what the subject is. [Cf. the same Reiske in the notes on Tarafa's Moallaka, p. 86.] Our Job himself used this figure above, ch. XXVI, 2-5, where he describes God without naming him. Compare XL, 10." So Reiske, with whom Doederlein in his Scholia ad Libros Poeticos V. T. on the passage, and Dathe agree; they translate these words thus: There is one that exults with whirring wings, etc. Whether this is to be preferred to the interpretation that Bochart will give presently, let each judge for himself. I pass over the bold conjectures of Reiske and Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer], by which they needlessly disturb the received text. Whoever wishes to know them should consult the authors themselves.

notes.text: The asseverative sense of the particle אם, which is perhaps the primary one, seems rather to be derived from the meaning to tend, to aim at, to have a purpose, which is found in the Arabic verb أَمَّ [amma], which ALB. SCHULTENS compared on Job 42:8, p. 1214. Cf. STORR, Observatt. ad Analog. et Synt. Hebr. p. 348, note *).

notes.text: I refrain from reviewing the opinions, or rather the guesses, of others in interpreting this verse, since this has already been done sufficiently by SCHULTENS in his Commentary on the passage, p. 1118 ff. The vain conjectures of Schmidt and Cocceius have also been refuted by TYMPIUS in his Annotationibus et Vindiciis on Noldii Concordantt. Particularr. p. 903 b, note 1460.
